Initially, AE is often asymptomatic, and the time from infection to the development of a typical AE-liver lesion is 5 to 15 years in immunocompetent individuals. Further confirmation derived from an immunohistochemical staining with the monoclonal antibody Em2G11 (Ulm, Germany) [23] (Fig. 1e) or by the detection of Em specific DNA by PCR method (Wien, Austria). Cytological analysis of samples gained by fine-needle aspiration biopsy was also carried out. Cytology alone without further confirmatory tests such as immunocytochemistry was regarded as ina

brolamellar carcinoma. Based on histopathological findings, the following preliminary diagnoses were made: granulomatous hepatitis, chronic hepatitis with fibrosis, helminthosis and echinococcosis. In 10 patients confirmed by histology, protoscoleces or hooklets were evident in two patients (20%) (Fig. 2c-d). In four patients (25%), immunohistochemistry (n = 2; 12.5%) and polymerase chain reaction (n = 2; 12.5%) were used to confirm diagnosis. Em antibodies were detected in 13 out of 16 patients (81.3%). Diagnostic delay ranged from 1 to 122 months (mean diagnostic delay: 33 months) (Table 1).

panels.figure_caption: Alveolar echinococcosis with infiltration into the liver capsule, diaphragm, and omentum. The patient had a liver mass in the right lobe and another mass in the left lobe. Laparoscopy: (A) Right lobe of the liver with extensive yellow, cake-like, cheesy material (straight arrows) covering the liver capsule. (B) Left lobe of the liver with yellow cheesy material (straight arrow), liver capsule, and diaphragm. (C) Omentum with infiltration by yellow cheesy material (curly arrow). (D) Cut surface of the right lobe showing the tumor mass (curly arrows) with tiny, sponge-like cysts (microvesicles).
in_text_mentions: er capsule and involved adjacent organs in nine patients (PNM N1). The adjacent organs included the right hemidiaphragm (n = 4), right adrenal gland (n = 4), omentum (n = 1), gastrohepatic ligament (n = 1), gallbladder (n = 1), stomach and duodenum (n = 2), and hilar lymph nodes (n = 2) (Figure 5). Lung metastases were seen in two patients and presented as multiple nodules of 3 mm to 1.5 cm (PNM M1). One of the patients had lymphadenopathy in the right hilum of the lung. Based on PNM classification, three patients had stage 1 disease, four had stage IIIb disease, and five had stage IV disease.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Caption states Ultrasound image of alveolar echinococcosis (AE) lesion in the liver for Patient No. 11, disease-focused article on emerging human AE. Real patient ultrasound visibly shows hepatic lesion. No ultrasound finding_key in vocabulary, so captured as proposed_findings. B: Caption identifies as Axial T1 weighted MR image of the same AE lesion in liver. Hypointense appearance consistent with fibroinflammatory matrix, identified visually. C: Caption gross picture of AE lesion removed by segmentectomy. Shows classic spongy multivesicular yellow lesion with necrotic areas. D: Caption microscopic appearance notes PAS positive laminated layer surrounded by necrotic material. In-text confirms laminated layer with necrosis and granulomatous reaction for Fig.1d-e. E: Caption IHC with Em2G11 marking laminated layer of E. multilocularis, specific confirmatory staining for AE.

in_text_mentions: growth pattern, mimicking malignancy. Histologically, AE-lesions are characterized by necrosis with intermingled fragments of the laminated layer surrounded by a granulomatous inflammation [3] (Fig. 1c; Fig. 2a). Initially, AE is often asymptomatic, and the time from infection to the development of a typical AE-liver lesion is 5 to 15 years in immunocompetent individuals. Diagnosis of AE is based on clinical and epidemiological data, imaging techniques, histopathology and/or nucleic acid detection and serology [7]. Imaging techniques has a central role in the differential diagnosis and clinic

lender (< 1 mm) laminated layer within abundant necrotic areas, a tubular growth pattern accompanied by a granulomatous cell-reaction without any definite fibrous capsule around the lesion [22] (Fig. 1d-e, Fig. 2b-d). Further confirmation derived from an immunohistochemical staining with the monoclonal antibody Em2G11 (Ulm, Germany) [23] (Fig. 1e) or by the detection of Em specific DNA by PCR method (Wien, Austria). Hypodense mass in the right lobe of the liver blocking a branch of the right portal vein (arrow). (E) CECT. Tumor mass in the right adrenal gland (arrow), with lymph nodes around IVC. (F) CT chest. Two nodular opacities in the right and left lungs (arrows).

The caption and image show rim-like FDG uptake at the lesion periphery with a photopenic center, the classic peripheral metabolic activity (active germinal layer uptake) of alveolar echinococcosis. [raw subtype: Kodama Type 3] B: Axial contrast-enhanced MRI of the same patient showing the large infiltrative hepatic alveolar echinococcosis lesion with peripheral contrast uptake and central nonenhancing cystic portions. panels.figure_caption: 45-year-old female patient with AE and involvement of liver segments IVa–VII and Kodama Type 3 lesion. Increased FDG uptake is observed at the lesion rim (A) with increased uptake of the contrast agent (B). High signal intensity is present in the central cystic parts in T2w imaging with fat suppression (C). Diffusion imaging demonstrates a high signal at a low b-value (b50) in the central parts of the lesion (D), a low signal at a high b-value (b800) (E), and high ADC values (F), indicative of no diffusion restriction.
in_text_mentions: The number of lesions was 22 (Type 1), 11 (Type 2), 13 (Type 3), 3 (Type 4), and 2 (Type 5, Table 3). Lesion size was significantly different between Kodama Types 1 vs. 3 and 2 vs. 3 (F = 5.4, p < 0.001 and <0.05, respectively, Figure 2A). SUVavg values were 2.1 ± 0.6 for Type 1, 3.4 ± 2.2 for Type 2, 4.1 ± 1.5 for Type 3, 4.2 ± 2.1 for Type 4, and 2.5 ± 1.4 for Type 5. Significant differences between Groups 1 and 3 were detected for SUVavg (F = 9.9, p < 0.003) and SUVmax (2.6 ± 0.8 and 5.0 ± 1.7, F = 9.3, p < 0.04). Patient examples are given in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

Caption: 'calcified and necrotic debris and dense periparasitic fibrosis ... chronic inflammation and fibrosis'; in-text: 'dense fibroconnective tissue ... multinucleated giant cells, and epithelioid histiocytes'.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Human kidney core biopsy H&E from the reported child; the caption and in-text identify Echinococcus multilocularis-type laminated membrane, cystic structures, calcific/necrotic debris, dense fibrosis and effaced renal parenchyma, supporting alveolar echinococcosis despite the absence of liver involvement. B: Lower-right inset from the same kidney core biopsy; the captioned thin laminar membrane measured on trichrome stain is a specific histologic feature of alveolar echinococcosis in this patient. C: Upper-left insert shows a captioned scolex from the kidney core-biopsy block; a scolex is parasite-specific evidence supporting alveolar echinococcosis, although this feature is not present in the allowed findings vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Joyce et al. Disseminated Echinococcus multilocularis Infection without Liver Involvement in Child, Canada, 2018.. Emerging infectious diseases 2020. doi:10.3201/eid2608.191644. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Kidney core biopsy of a child with disseminated Echinococcus multilocularis infection without liver involvement, Canada, 2018. Shown are folded laminated membrane (short black arrows) encircling variable-sized cystic structures (black circles) containing calcified and necrotic debris and dense periparasitic fibrosis (long black arrows), in a background of chronic inflammation and fibrosis. No residual normal kidney parenchyma was seen (hematoxylin and eosin stain, original magnification × 40). Inset at lower right shows laminar membrane, 18–19.4 μm in thickness in a background of fibrosis (Masson trichrome, original magnification ×40). Insert at upper left shows scolex attached to the paraffin edge of the block (original magnification ×40).
in_text_mentions: e biopsies showed a predominantly solid lesion composed of dense fibroconnective tissue and containing macrophages, myofibroblasts, occasional multinucleated giant cells, and epithelioid histiocytes (Figure 2). In a few cores, there was evidence of variable-sized cystic structures encircled by a thin laminated layer with a thickness of 17–39.6 μm, as measured on Masson trichrome special stain (Figure 2). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: PAS-stained human liver histology showing the classic five-zone structure of alveolar echinococcosis: central laminated layer (a) with necrotic zone 1, epithelioid/granulocyte layer 2, fibrotic zone 3, lymphocyte layer 4, and adjacent liver tissue 5. B: PAS-stained human liver histology showing zone 3b, an outer fibrotic rim with lymphocyte infiltrates (arrow) between zones 4 and 5, a feature particularly apparent in EMUC-CT type III alveolar echinococcosis lesions. [raw subtype: EMUC-CT type III] C: High-magnification PAS-stained human liver histology of the acellular laminated layer of Echinococcus multilocularis with width measurements (brackets a and b), the classic diagnostic histological feature of alveolar echinococcosis.

(B): An example of zone 3b, which is particularly apparent in Echinococcus multilocularis Ulm Classification for Computed Tomography (EMUC-CT) type III lesions. This zone comprises an additional fibrotic rim between zone 4 and zone 5. Lymphocyte infiltrates can also be found in zone 3b (arrow) (a: laminated layer; 1: necrotic zone; 2–4: border zone; 5: liver host tissue; 3b: outer fibrotic rim). (C): Examples of laminated layer width measurements (indicated with white brackets labelled a and b) in Periodic Schiff staining (PAS)-stained tissue (a = 26.7 µm; b = 14.1 µm).

in_text_mentions: on. Partial cystectomy was performed for pancreatic lesion and hypertonic saline (15%) was drainage into the cyst for a minimum duration of 10 min. Histologic examination revealed diagnosis of hepatic and pancreatic alveolar echinococcosis (AE) with scolex seen in the fibrous tissues (Fig. 2). The postoperative course was uneventful and the patient was discharged on the 5th of postoperative day and then continued 2-year albendazole therapy. He was well followed up at our outpatient department with serologic tests and imaging procedures, and no recurrence was occurred 8 years after the surgery.

in_text_mentions: The pathological result using the lesion sample (covered by liver tissue) showed that the lesion was probably hepatic alveolar echinococcosis, as it showed very obvious central liquefied necrosis regions (Figure 2). However, in contrast to what was described in the literature, the striation of the laminated layer was moderate rather than weak, and the color was pink instead of bluish-clear, as described in the literature for AE lesions in H&E staining [12].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Low-power HE of the explanted liver showing E. multilocularis metacestodes with calcifications, eosinophilic laminated layer fragments (in-text citation to Figure 4A) and adjacent severe fibrosis - all components of the alveolar echinococcosis lesion spectrum described in the caption; not PSC, since no onion-skin fibrosis, ductopenia or piecemeal necrosis is described. B: Low-power HE showing metacestodes largely destroyed by the host inflammatory response with dense fibrous reaction; the caption frames it as part of the spectrum of E. multilocularis lesion histology, supporting alveolar echinococcosis attribution. C: High-power HE showing granulomas with eosinophils, the classic granulomatous host reaction to Echinococcus multilocularis metacestodes in the explanted liver, as described in the caption's spectrum of lesion features. D: High-power HE of the lesion showing abscess formation; the in-text explicitly cites Figure 4D...
panels.attribution_text: Fronhoffs et al. Alveolar Echinococcosis in a Patient with Presumed Autoimmune Hepatitis and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis: An Unexpected Finding after Liver Transplantation.. Pathogens (Basel, Switzerland) 2023. doi:10.3390/pathogens12010073. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: (A–F): Spectrum of histological features of the lesions. Some metacestodes contained calcifications, while the adjacent liver tissue showed severe fibrosis with loose lymphocytic infiltrate ((A), HE, ×40). Other metacestodes were largely destroyed by inflammation ((B), HE, ×12.5). Areas with granulomas and eosinophils ((C), HE, ×200), abscess formation ((D), HE, ×200) or numerous plasma cells ((E), HE, ×200), many of them IgG4-positive ((F), ×100), were present.
in_text_mentions: In some areas, the adjacent liver tissue was fibrotic or hemorrhagic. The histology of the explanted liver revealed multiple metacestodes of Echinococcus multilocularis with fragments of the eosinophilic laminated layers (Figure 2C,D and Figure 4A,D. The amount of IgG4-positive plasma cells was strikingly increased (Figure 4F).

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: 'The mass shows a multiloculated cyst with a germinal layer (arrows): (a) HE stain'
In-text: 'a liver biopsy was performed, showing granulomatous demarcated necrosis zones'

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Human liver biopsy histology (HE) from a patient with confirmed alveolar echinococcosis (positive E. multilocularis serology, article title and caption explicitly state alveolar echinococcosis). The image shows the characteristic multiloculated cyst with a germinal/laminated layer indicated by red arrows, and surrounding granulomatous demarcated necrosis as described in the text. Classic textbook histopathology of the disease. b: Human liver biopsy histology (PAS stain) from the same patient with confirmed alveolar echinococcosis. The PAS stain demonstrates the PAS-positive laminated cuticular/germinal membranes characteristic of Echinococcus multilocularis infection, with red arrows indicating the membranes. Disease attribution is explicit in the caption and supported by positive serology in the text.
panels.attribution_text: Diem et al. Accelerated Course of Alveolar Echinococcosis After Treatment With Steroids in a Patient With Autoimmune Encephalitis.. Cureus 2021. doi:10.7759/cureus.18831. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Liver biopsy showing alveolar echinococcosis The mass shows a multiloculated cyst with a germinal layer (arrows): (a) HE stain, (b) PAS stain. Abbreviations: HE = hematoxylin-eosin, PAS = periodic acid-Schiff
in_text_mentions: The CT scan of October 2020 showed new onset of multiple hypodense lesions of the liver, primarily suspected as metastases, compared to the CT of June 2020 (Figure 1). Therefore, a liver biopsy was performed, showing granulomatous demarcated necrosis zones and evidence of amorphous cuticular membranes with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positivity compatible with Echinococcus spp. infestation (Figure 2). Malignancy could be excluded. The serology testing for Echinococcus multilocularis was positive (Table 1).

panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance imaging findings. (A) T1-weighted images show hypointense lesions (blue arrow), while (B) T2-weighted images demonstrate a hypointense peripheral rim (blue arrow) with central hyperintensity (yellow arrow). Mild peripheral contrast enhancement is visible in the arterial phase (C), becoming more pronounced in the delayed phases (D). Perfusion reduction secondary to portal vein thrombosis (E, blue arrow), along with a heterogeneous parenchymal appearance (F, blue arrow).
in_text_mentions: hyperintensity on T2-weighted images. Persistent peripheral contrast enhancement was observed across all dynamic phases, accompanied by perfusion abnormalities in the surrounding hepatic parenchyma (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) confirmed the presence of peripheral calcifications, invasion of the posterior branch of the right portal vein, and markedly reduced perfusion (Figure 2). in_text_mentions: enhancement was observed across all dynamic phases, accompanied by perfusion abnormalities in the surrounding hepatic parenchyma (Figure 1). Computed tomography (CT) confirmed the presence of peripheral calcifications, invasion of the posterior branch of the right portal vein, and markedly reduced perfusion (Figure 2). Positron emission tomography CT revealed intense fluorodeoxyglucose uptake around the lesions (SUVmax: 8.9), consistent with active inflammation. Collectively, these findings suggested hepatic alveolar echinococcosis (HAE), which was subsequently confirmed by positive serology.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Precontrast axial CT of a 53-year-old female with a hepatic AE lesion showing irregular borders and calcification (arrow), matching the classic infiltrative calcified hepatic mass pattern of alveolar echinococcosis described in the disease-focused article. B: Portal venous axial CT of the same hepatic AE lesion showing a non-enhancing lesion with central necrosis (black star), calcification (arrows) and perilesional enhancement (white star) — the classic contrast CT appearance of hepatic alveolar echinococcosis.

panels.figure_caption: 53-year-old female. Hepatic lesion with irregular borders and calcification (A,B—arrows) on precontrast axial CT (A). On portal venous images (B), no enhancement is present in the lesion. Central necrosis can be seen (B—black star). Perilesional enhancement (B—white star) is present.
in_text_mentions: The most frequently encountered CT pattern was a heterogeneous mass with calcifications and hypoattenuating areas (72.3%). Most of the lesions had irregular contours (85.4%), 85.4% lacked contrast enhancement, 77.4% of the lesions had calcifications, and atrophy and capsular retraction was present in 10.7% of the lesions (Figure 2 and Figure 3). Table 3 details the distribution of CT appearances.

The mean ADC value of hepatic AE lesions’ solid components was 1.51 ± 0.32 × 10−3 mm2/s (range: 0.97–1.78 × 10−3 mm2/s) (Figure 3). Table 5 summarizes the mean ADC values for the various types of AE lesions.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Precontrast axial CT of a 51-year-old male with a hepatic alveolar echinococcosis lesion showing irregular contours, dystrophic calcifications, central necrosis and capsular retraction, consistent with the article's imaging series of hepatic AE. B: Portal venous phase axial CT of the same hepatic AE lesion showing a nonenhancing necrotic core, perilesional enhancement and capsular retraction, matching the article's description of untreated hepatic alveolar echinococcosis.

panels.figure_caption: 51-year-old male. Hepatic lesion with irregular contours and calcifications on precontrast axial CT (A). On portal venous images (B), no enhancement is present in the lesion. in_text_mentions: The most frequently encountered CT pattern was a heterogeneous mass with calcifications and hypoattenuating areas (72.3%). Most of the lesions had irregular contours (85.4%), 85.4% lacked contrast enhancement, 77.4% of the lesions had calcifications, and atrophy and capsular retraction was present in 10.7% of the lesions (Figure 2 and Figure 3). Table 3 details the distribution of CT appearances.

in_text_mentions: The most frequently encountered MRI pattern was a heterogeneous mass with irregular contours with central necrosis (78.7%). in_text_mentions: At present, in addition to fine needle biopsy, we have no suitable examination method to monitor early HAE lesions with a diameter <3 cm (37). Therefore, it is of great significance to improve the understanding of sonographers on early HAE. Hemangioma-like changes and hailstorm sign are the early characteristics of HAE, and calcification is a common concomitant sign. Because the samples in this study came from clinically diagnosed cases and were not pathologically confirmed, further in-depth study with large samples is needed (see Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial contrast CT from a surgical series of hepatic alveolar echinococcosis. The red arrow marks an infiltrative honeycomb AE lesion in the right anterior lobe, matching the configured disease. The same slice also shows a well-circumscribed CE cyst (white arrow) in the right posterior lobe, but that is a concomitant different-disease finding and does not negate the clearly captioned AE lesion, so the panel is included for alveolar echinococcosis. No age/ethnicity stated for this patient. B: Axial contrast CT showing the red-arrow AE lesion in the middle liver lobe with a multivesicular/honeycomb infiltrative architecture, a classic CT manifestation of hepatic alveolar echinococcosis. Real patient preoperative diagnostic image from an AE hepatectomy series; no other disease is shown in this panel. No age or ethnicity stated for this patient.

in_text_mentions: I was 22.8 kg/m2 (18–33 kg/m2). None of the patients had clinical discomfort when they sought medical attention, except two patients who had dull pain in the right upper abdomen preoperatively. The serology results of all patients were positive, and the residual liver volume were adequate (>40%) by preoperative imaging assessment. No patient had received albendazole treatment before surgery. Of note, the fifth patient was also found to have a CE cyst on the right liver lobe in addition to an AE lesion, and the AE lesion of the eleventh patient was located within the middle liver lobe (Fig. 1).

in_text_mentions: The number of lesions was 22 (Type 1), 11 (Type 2), 13 (Type 3), 3 (Type 4), and 2 (Type 5, Table 3). SUVavg values were 2.1 ± 0.6 for Type 1, 3.4 ± 2.2 for Type 2, 4.1 ± 1.5 for Type 3, 4.2 ± 2.1 for Type 4, and 2.5 ± 1.4 for Type 5. Significant differences between Groups 1 and 3 were detected for SUVavg (F = 9.9, p < 0.003) and SUVmax (2.6 ± 0.8 and 5.0 ± 1.7, F = 9.3, p < 0.04). panels.rationale: Single coronal contrast-enhanced abdominal CT of a child with disseminated Echinococcus multilocularis infection (the cause of alveolar echinococcosis), explicitly without liver involvement. The red arrow marks a large irregular hypodense left renal lesion corresponding to a centrally necrotic, nonenhancing alveolar echinococcal mass, satisfying the nonenhancing-necrotic-core CT finding. The white arrow marks a partially visualized porto-systemic shunt, which is recorded as a proposed finding because it is not in the allowed vocabulary. The presentation is atypical for alveolar echinococcosis because the disease characteristically involves the liver, whereas this case is explicitly hepatic-sparing with renal manifestation. Real human diagnostic radiology, not third-party, with arrow annotations present.

A Hailstorm: irregular shape, indistinct margins, heterogeneous internal echoes with hyperechoic foci and posterior shadowing; B Hemangioma-like: well-demarcated lesion with high or slightly high echogenicity and uniform or heterogeneous internal echoes; C Pseudocystic: hyperechoic rim, unclear borders, peripheral echo heterogeneity, thick cyst wall (> 10 mm), and hypoechoic or anechoic center; D Metastasis-like: hypoechoic lesion resembling colorectal liver metastases, often with a hypoechoic halo and heterogeneous central echotexture; E Ossification: solitary or clustered lesions with sharp margins and prominent dorsal acoustic shadowing due to calcification or ossification. Representative ultrasound images are provided for each subtype

source_variant.figure_caption: Ultrasound patterns of hepatic alveolar echinococcosis categorized using the Echinococcus multilocularis Ulm Classification-Ultrasound (EMUC-US) system. A Hailstorm: irregular shape, indistinct margins, heterogeneous internal echoes with hyperechoic foci and posterior shadowing; B Hemangioma-like: well-demarcated lesion with high or slightly high echogenicity and uniform or heterogeneous internal echoes; C Pseudocystic: hyperechoic rim, unclear borders, peripheral echo heterogeneity, thick cyst wall (> 10 mm), and hypoechoic or anechoic center; D Metastasis-like: hypoechoic lesion resembling colorectal liver metastases, often with a hypoechoic halo and heterogeneous central echotexture; E Ossification: solitary or clustered lesions with sharp margins and prominent dorsal acoustic shadowing due to calcification or ossification. Representative ultrasound images are provided for each subtype

in_text_mentions: 35 lesions in 8 patients diagnosed with CAE, as outlined in Table 2. The findings demonstrated that 11C-CHO PET/CT successfully detected all 35 lesions, achieving a 100% accuracy rate. This contrasted with the performance of 18F-FDG PET/CT, which only identified 24 lesions, resulting in an accuracy rate of 68.57%. Quantitative analysis further indicated that the SUVmax for 11C-CHO PET/CT averaged 3.13 ± 0.93, compared to 9.35 ± 2.84 for 18F-FDG PET/CT. The average size of the lesion was 3.198 × 2.631 cm on 18F-FDG, 2.615 × 2.234 cm on 11C-CHO, and 2.535 × 2.183 cm on MRI (as showed in Fig. 2).

panels.figure_caption: 18F-FDG and 11C-CHO PET/CT imaging a 37-year-old female patient underwent brain 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging following a seizure episode. The scan revealed multiple mixed-density nodules in the brain. Some nodules exhibited significantly lower radioactive uptake than brain tissue, while others displayed uptake levels similar to brain tissue. The SUVmax was 14.1 (compared to the normal brain tissue SUVmax of 14.7), as depicted in A and B. Subsequently, the patient underwent brain 11C-CHO PET/CT imaging the following day, revealing multiple mixed-density nodules, all exhibiting higher radioactive uptake than the brain background. The SUVmax was 3.9 (compared to the normal brain tissue SUVmax of 0.2), as shown in C and D. Ultimately, the patient underwent surgical resection, and pathological examination confirmed CAE, as illustrated in E and F. 18F-FDG = 18F-fludeoxyglucose, PET/CT = positron emission tomography/computed tomography.
in_text_mentions: 11C-CHO in CAE lesions showed varying degrees of uptake on PET/CT images. Thirteen CAE lesions with 11C-CHO uptake showing a concentrated blocky radioactive distribution; 11 lesions with 11C-CHO showing a ring-shaped concentrated radioactive distribution around the CAE lesions; 11 lesions with 11C-CHO uptake showing radioactive distribution in CAE lesions with defects and sparse areas (as showed in Fig. 1).

panels.rationale: Autopsy gross specimen of a human lung from a case report of progressive alveolar echinococcosis; caption and in-text confirm cystic, partly calcified and centrally necrotized infiltrations of both lungs. The multivesicular cystic architecture and central necrotic/hemorrhagic lesions are characteristic gross manifestations of alveolar echinococcosis, while gross calcified foci (black asterisks) have no matching gross-category vocabulary entry and are proposed as an additional finding.

in_text_mentions: ricin B (3 mg/kg daily) was added as anthelmintic salvage therapy. Despite using all technical facilities the patient died of respiratory insufficiency after 20 days at the intensive care unit. Autopsy confirmed cystic, partly calcified and centrally necrotized infiltrations of both lungs (Figure 1), the liver and the brain. Histology of the brain, the lung and the liver revealed large cystic lesions with eosinophilic brood capsules, scolices and daughter cysts. The cysts were surrounded by dense fibrovascular tissue with chronic inflammatory cells and showed a varying degree of calcification.

panels.rationale: Single axial T2-weighted MRI from an open-access case report of alveolar echinococcosis. The image and caption show the patient's own AE lesion: a large infiltrative honeycomb hepatic mass in the right liver lobe with microcystic (grape-like) and necrotic components abutting the right pedicle, with anatomic labels (Li, Co, Pa, LK, A, IVC) marking the AE tumor (*). This is a real human-patient image of the configured disease, so the panel is included.
panels.attribution_text: Golriz et al. Case Report: Successful DaVinci-Assisted Major Liver Resection for Alveolar Echinococcosis.. Frontiers in surgery 2021. doi:10.3389/fsurg.2021.639304. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: MRI imaging showing the AE lesion of our patient in the axial plane. Li, liver; Co, colon; Pa, pancreas; LK, left kidney; A, aorta; IVC, inferior vena cava, *AE tumor.
in_text_mentions: nd 26–28 kDa proteins in size. Blood tumor markers were in the normal range (CEA: 0.7 ug/l, CA 19–9: 23.4 U/ml, and AFP: 2.1 IU/ml). MRI imaging showed an enormous manifestation of AE in the right liver with microcystic and necrotic components that contacted the right pedicle (Figure 1); no further suspicious lesions were present in the liver or lymph nodes. There were no distant metastases (head, chest). Our multidisciplinary liver board discussed the case and recommended radical surgical resection of the lesion with a right-sided hemihepatectomy and parasitostatic treatment with albendazole.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E paraffin section of the resected liver lesion (200x). Caption states histopathology of liver lesion and that the arrows indicate AE; in-text confirms final pathology consistent with AE. The arrow points to a laminated cyst wall and the surrounding tissue shows a scirrhous granulomatous reaction with fibrosis, both characteristic of alveolar echinococcosis. B: High-power H&E of the liver lesion (400x). The black arrow indicates an AE laminated/germinal membrane, surrounded by fibroinflammatory stroma. Caption and in-text pathology report attribute this lesion to alveolar echinococcosis in a multiorgan resection case. C: H&E of the resected kidney lesion (200x). Caption labels this as kidney histopathology with arrows indicating AE, and the article describes multiorgan (hepatic and renal) alveolar echinococcosis resection. The arrowed round laminated cyst wall and surrounding granulomatous fibrosis are characteristic of AE. D:...

panels.rationale: Axial contrast abdominal CT from a human patient in a case report of disseminated alveolar echinococcosis with positive E. multilocularis serology (ELISA and Western blot for EgP, EgHF, Em18). The image shows a large infiltrative multivesicular hepatic mass with perilesional calcifications and vascular compression/occlusion, which are hallmark CT features of alveolar echinococcosis. Disease attribution is strongly supported by the disease-focused article title, the specific captioned manifestations, and the confirmatory serology described in the in-text mentions.

in_text_mentions: Patient underwent contrast enhanced CT (Figs. 1, 2, 3, 4). In IV, VIII and partially V segments of the liver was detected irregularly shaped volumetric formation with signs of infiltrative growth in the surrounding parenchyma of the liver, with fuzzy uneven contours, cystic-solid structure, heterogeneous density from + 10 to + 40 HU. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: T2-weighted axial MRI of a 68-year-old man's liver (segment IV) showing the characteristic multivesicular bunch-of-grapes structure of alveolar echinococcosis with a solid matrix component, directly attributed to AE in the caption. b: T2-weighted coronal MRI of the same AE patient showing the grape-like microvesicular lesion with bile duct infiltration and consecutive biliary dilatation, matching the caption's description of alveolar echinococcosis. c: T1-weighted post-gadolinium axial MRI of the AE lesion showing the hypointense fibroinflammatory solid matrix with infiltrative ill-defined margins and faint peripheral enhancement, a typical MRI feature of alveolar echinococcosis per the caption. d: Coronal CT of the same patient explicitly showing the typical coarse (geographic dystrophic) calcification of alveolar echinococcosis, with a honeycomb infiltrative hepatic mass and necrotic cavity, as stated in the caption.

panels.figure_caption: T2-weighted axial (a) and coronal (b) MR images show the characteristic multivesicular structure of alveolar echinococcosis (AE) located in the fourth liver segment detected in a 68-year-old man. The lesion is composed of multiple small cysts surrounding a solid component (a,b, stars) and a large irregular cyst. Note the extension into the left liver lobe with bile duct infiltration and consecutive biliary dilatation (a–d, triangles). The correspondent T1-weighted axial MR image (c) after intravenous gadolinium injection shows the typical faint enhancement at the periphery of the lesion (c, arrows) and the infiltrative character because of ill-defined margins, particularly well seen in the posterior part of this lesion, explaining the frequent misdiagnosis as a tumor. The coronal CT-image of the same patient (d) nicely demonstrates the typical coarse calcification of AE (c, arrow).
in_text_mentions: agnosis relies on a combination of imaging and serology. Ultrasonography (US) is the first-line examination, while magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) further characterize the lesion and its invasion of surrounding structures. The characteristic radiological features on CT and MRI are illustrated in Figure 1. Additional imaging (thoracic CT, brain MRI) is recommended to assess distant dissemination, while (Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography) PET-CT is useful for determining the metabolic activity of lesions, which correlates with parasite viability [18].

in_text_mentions: herefore the antibiotic treatment was changed to Amoxicillin. Owing to drug hypersensitivity, the treatment had to be changed to Vancomycine and Zyvoxid. During hospitalization the patient developed additional pain in the upper lumbar spine from lumbar vertebrae L1 to L3 without neurological deficit. Simultaneously the general health condition of the patient worsened. A CT examination of the lumbar spine showed geographic bone destruction and inhomogeneous osteolysis of the lumbar vertebra L1 to L3 without soft tissue involvement, leading to the diagnosis of osteomyelitis (see figure 1 and 2).

ific. Inhomogeneous osteolysis and irregular bone destruction may be seen. In the soft tissues, CT can reveal cystic masses with irregular thickened septations [14]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may show tube-like cavities/cystic lesions with a multi-vesicular morphology if soft tissue is infected. Diagnostic criteria for cystic lesions are high intensity on T2-weighted images and low intensity on T1-weighted images without contrast agent enhancement (see figure 2). Because of the contrast enhancing thickened margins and septations AE can easily be confused with abscess formations [15,16].

panels.rationale: Axial thoracic CT from the case report, explicitly captioned and in-text described as a 45 mm recurrent alveolar echinococcosis lesion in the right pulmonary apex after a 1982 right lobectomy; disease attribution is unambiguous (caption, in-text, article title, and prior triage all support AE, no third-party issue). A small hyperdense calcific focus is visible within the circled, caliper-measured apical lesion, supporting the CT calcification finding; the pulmonary apical recurrence itself is not represented in the hepatic/MRI/gross/histology vocabulary and is captured as a proposed finding. Pulmonary involvement is a recognized but less common (variant) manifestation versus classic hepatic AE.

Real patient radiology, no third-party copyright. B: CT image of the same human patient with alveolar echinococcosis. Caption states hepatic lesion and pericardial fluid with a white arrowhead indicating echinococcal invasion of the pericardium, and the article title describes AE of the liver that ruptured into the pericardium. Rupture into the pericardium is an unusual complication, hence atypical. Pericardial fluid/effusion and pericardial invasion are not in the provided vocabulary and are listed as proposed findings.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Contrast CT panel from a patient with hepatic alveolar echinococcosis, showing calcified fibrotic infiltration of left diaphragm and spleen plus left pleural effusion/cyst; extrahepatic involvement makes it a variant presentation. B: T1-weighted post-contrast MRI shows hypovascular fibrotic/inflammatory infiltration extending from liver to left diaphragm due to alveolar echinococcosis; direct panel-specific attribution to AE. C: T2-weighted coronal MRI shows fibrotic infiltration of left diaphragm/spleen and left pleural effusion due to alveolar echinococcosis; extrahepatic spread is a less common complicated presentation. D: Post-contrast T1 MRI shows classic confluent echinococcal cysts and fibrotic infiltration in both liver lobes due to alveolar echinococcosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial chest CT of the reported alveolar echinococcosis patient showing multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, consistent with metastatic pulmonary spread of AE; caption states multiple lesions in bilateral lung (A,B). B: Axial chest CT at a lower level showing further bilateral pulmonary lesions in the same confirmed alveolar echinococcosis patient; caption attributes the bilateral lung lesions to the disease workup. C: Abdominal CT showing a large infiltrative hypodense hepatic lesion, the classic primary site of alveolar echinococcosis; caption and in-text confirm liver lesions in this AE case with positive hydatid IgG and biopsy of the liver mass. D: Abdominal CT with yellow arrow highlighting obvious thickening of the right adrenal gland in the same alveolar echinococcosis patient; adrenal involvement is a less common disseminated manifestation, hence variant typicality.

Hypodense lesion with uneven enhancement indicating nonenhancing necrotic/cystic core on contrast CT
Mixed density lesion with uneven enhancement in the L1 vertebra and paraspinal tissue; mixed signal on MRI consistent with hypointense fibroinflammatory matrix component
Lamellar structure with positive periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) positive staining, corresponding to PAS-positive laminated cyst wall
Granulomatous inflammation with necrosis on liver biopsy, corresponding to necrotizing granulomatous reaction

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial contrast CT of liver showing a large hypodense infiltrative lesion with uneven enhancement in the right posterior lobe, consistent with hepatic alveolar echinococcosis. B: Axial contrast CT showing ring-enhancing cystic lesions in the right abdominal wall connected to the intrahepatic lesion, representing disseminated alveolar echinococcosis. C: Sagittal enhanced MRI of thoracic and lumbar spine showing a mixed-density lesion with uneven enhancement in L1 vertebra and paraspinal tissue, representing spinal dissemination of alveolar echinococcosis. A: Panel A is an axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT from a case report of confirmed alveolar echinococcosis, showing the large space-occupying lesion in the right hepatic lobe described in the caption. B: Panel B is the same contrast-enhanced abdominal CT series showing the second space-occupying lesion in the left hepatic lobe of the patient with alveolar echinococcosis. Caption only describes a space-occupying lesion, so disease attribution depends on the article's case-report context and is therefore of moderate confidence.

in_text_mentions: A 32-year-old male presented to the emergency unit with epigastralgia and weight loss over the past year. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) in the portal phase depicted a diffuse involvement of the left hepatic lobe by a confluent necrotic mass with irregular margins and peripheral scattered calcifications (Figure 1—yellow arrow).
A second location of 8 cm was present in the left cardiophrenic recess (Figure 1—orange arrow) and a third mediastinal (not shown). This pattern is compatible with hepatic alveolar echinococcosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial T2 fat-sat MRI shows a cystic lobulated multivesicular lesion in the right medial parotid gland (arrow) in an article focused on alveolar echinococcosis of the parotid gland; the bunch-of-grapes microcystic MRI pattern supports the finding, while the parotid location is ultra-rare and therefore atypical. B: Coronal T2 fat-sat MRI confirms the same cystic lobulated multivesicular parotid lesion (arrow) in the article's alveolar echinococcosis of the parotid gland; the microcystic bunch-of-grapes pattern fits the vocabulary, and the parotid site is explicitly ultra-rare, so presentation is atypical.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real-patient thoracic CT from the confirmed alveolar echinococcosis case, showing bilateral non-cavitary nodular lesions with some calcifications, as stated in the caption and in-text report. Pulmonary dissemination is a less common presentation, so typicality is variant. The pulmonary findings are not represented by the supplied vocabulary and are therefore proposed as short clinical terms. B: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT of the confirmed alveolar echinococcosis patient shows a heterogeneous, irregular hepatic mass with calcifications and cystic components, supported by the caption, in-text description, and article title. These imaging features match the supplied infiltrative honeycomb hepatic mass and dystrophic calcification findings.
